Only `workspace_inspect`, `settings_search`, `settings_get`, `settings_preview_patch`, and `settings_apply_patch` are MCP-visible. `duplicate_object` and `inspect_selection` remain in-app fixtures pending an in-app eval; they are not callable over MCP. There is no MCP attachment-import contract.

Settings search/read cover the active FFF process preset. The write allowlist is `layer_height`, `wall_loops`, `sparse_infill_density`, `sparse_infill_pattern`, `top_shell_layers`, `bottom_shell_layers`, and `brim_width`. Apply takes `changes`, `expectedSessionId`, and `expectedRevision` from a fresh preview. Native approval captures the exact before/after values, including normalization dependencies, then revalidates before applying. It publishes one `Settings` revision, updates native fields and dirty state, and invalidates slicing. Use Orca preset revert or a previewed inverse patch to restore values; ordinary project Undo does not reverse preset edits.

The OpenAI adapter preserves the registry schemas and uses non-strict function calling for optional arguments or dynamic patch maps, which OpenAI strict mode cannot express. Native registry validation remains authoritative. Stateless Responses continuations retain user context and all prior tool results; the live multi-tool regression covers this path.

Update the actual table when implementation changes names, limits, or ownership. The source registry remains authoritative; this table explains why the surface exists.

## Process-settings tools: contract and hazards

The settings tools are the reference implementation of this guide. What
follows is the part of their design that stays true after the work is done;
the implementation handoff that produced it is retired. Re-read this section
before expanding the write allowlist or adding a tool that changes a preset.

### Standing decisions

1. Settings are data: four generic tools over searchable records, never one
   tool per setting.
2. Only the active FFF process preset's edited configuration is in scope. No
   `scope` field, and no printer, filament, plate, object, or modifier layer
   until each is a separately tested capability.
3. Metadata, parsing, and serialization come from Orca's own
   `print_config_def` and config option machinery. There is no parallel table
   of types, enum values, ranges, units, or aliases.
4. Search and read cover every process-setting definition; mutation is a
   reviewed allowlist. Every search and read record says whether the key is
   writable; other keys return `unsupported_setting_mutation`. Expand the list
   only after the real-adapter tests cover the option type, its dependency
   behavior, and the visible UI update for each new key.
5. A batch applies whole or not at all, through `Tab::load_config`, the path
   Orca itself uses to load a config into a preset. Never mutate the config
   behind the visible preset UI and imitate the notifications.
6. Process preset edits are not in project Undo. Results say so and return
   the previous values so a caller can propose the inverse.
7. A preview that finds invalid settings is a successful call with
   `valid: false`. Malformed input is a tool error.
8. All values cross JSON as strings in their canonical Orca serialization;
   callers may send numbers or booleans and the decoder converts them. All
   Orca ids cross JSON as strings.

### Error codes

| Condition | Code |
|---|---|
| key not in the definition table | `unknown_setting` with suggestions |
| key not a process option | `unsupported_scope` |
| readable key outside the allowlist | `unsupported_setting_mutation` |
| parse failure, bound violation, or layer height outside the printer's range | `invalid_setting_value` with `allowed` or bounds |
| spiral-mode conflict or a validator message on a touched key | `incompatible_settings` with the conflicting keys |
| session or revision mismatch, or a before value moved since preview | `stale_workspace` with expected and current |
| user rejected in JusPrin | `approval_rejected` |
| client cancelled or the app closed | `cancelled` |
| no FFF project or no process preset | `workspace_unavailable` |
| the batch call failed after validation | `execution_failed` |
| malformed arguments | `invalid_arguments` |

Preview never fails for content reasons. Apply fails with the first blocking
code and mutates nothing. Never convert an invariant failure into success.

### Orca entry points the tools use

- **Atomic batch:** `Tab::load_config(const DynamicPrintConfig&)` in
  `src/slic3r/GUI/Tab.cpp` diffs against the edited preset, sets every changed
  key, then runs `update_dirty()`, `reload_config()`, and `update()` once.
  `TabPrint::update()` runs the FFF normalizer and reaches
  `Plater::on_config_change`, which invalidates slicing as a sidebar edit
  would. Apply is therefore: build a config holding only the changed keys and
  call `wxGetApp().get_tab(Preset::TYPE_PRINT)->load_config(diff)`.
- **Parsing:** clone the edited config and `set_deserialize(key, text)` per
  key; Orca throws for unknown keys and unparseable values. Canonical value is
  `option->serialize()` after parsing.
- **Bounds and enums:** `ConfigOptionDef` in `src/libslic3r/Config.hpp`
  (`type`, `label`, `category`, `tooltip`, `sidetext`, `min`, `max`, `mode`,
  `readonly`, `enum_values`, `enum_labels`). Treat `min` and `max` as absent
  when they are the float limits.
- **Validation:** `Slic3r::validate(const FullPrintConfig&)` in
  `src/libslic3r/PrintConfig.cpp`, fed from `preset_bundle->full_config()`
  with the patched keys applied. Messages for touched keys are blocking;
  messages for untouched keys are warnings, because the preset was already
  invalid. `Print::validate` is a slicing-time check and is not part of
  preview, as in Orca's own UI.
- **Dirty state:** `PresetCollection::current_dirty_options()` and
  `current_different_from_parent_options()`; the preset name is
  `prints.get_edited_preset().name`. The Tab's per-option revert buttons read
  the same data, so they keep working after a tool apply.

### The normalizer can open dialogs and rewrite values

`update_print_fff_config` and `toggle_print_fff_options` in
`src/slic3r/GUI/ConfigManipulation.cpp` run inside `TabPrint::update()` after
every batch and evaluate every rule against the whole post-batch config, not
only the changed keys. Some rules open a modal dialog and then rewrite a
value; others rewrite silently. A modal opened from inside a tool execution
blocks the GUI thread while the request waits, and a silent rewrite makes the
result lie unless it is reported.

Two rules follow. Preview evaluates the same rule set against a clone, using
the printer preset and filament count the adapter can read, so a rule that
fires because of a pre-existing value is reported too. Dialog rules are
blocking issues; silent rules are warnings that name the dependent key and
its predicted value (`normalized_dependency`), and apply lists the actual
rewrite under `normalized`. Preview reuses Orca's `ConfigManipulation` on the
clone with no presentation callbacks rather than copying its option tables.

Rules reachable through the current allowlist, as audited when the tools
were built. Line numbers drift; search for the condition text.

| Rule in Orca | Reached by | Effect | Preview must |
|---|---|---|---|
| `layer_height` at or below epsilon | `layer_height` | modal, reset to 0.2 | refuse with `invalid_setting_value` and the minimum |
| `layer_height` above the printer's `max_layer_height` when that exceeds 0.2 | `layer_height` | modal, clamp | refuse with `invalid_setting_value` and the printer's maximum |
| `seam_slope_type` not `None` and absolute `seam_slope_start_height` at or above `layer_height` | lowering `layer_height` | modal, start height reset to 0 | refuse with `incompatible_settings`; evaluate percent values through `get_abs_value`, 100% or above also trips it |
| `spiral_mode` on and not all of `wall_loops` 1, `top_shell_layers` 0, `sparse_infill_density` 0 | those three keys | yes/no dialog, several keys rewritten either way | refuse with `incompatible_settings` naming `spiral_mode` |
| `sparse_infill_pattern` without multiline support while `fill_multiline` is above 1 | `sparse_infill_pattern` | silent: `fill_multiline` reset to 1 | predict and report as `normalized_dependency` |
| support-gap rounding block | none; it is inside `#if 0` | inactive | do not predict a change that does not happen |

Every active dialog predicate must be checked, including pre-existing
invalid ironing spacing, first-layer height, XY and elephant-foot
compensation, alternate-extra-wall, infill-lock depth, and fuzzy-skin
settings; spiral mode also checks support, enforced support layers, thin
walls, overhang reversal, timelapse, and wrapping detection. The real-adapter
test asserts that no top-level dialog appears during apply for any
allowlisted key under every row above, and that every predicted silent
rewrite appears in the result with its actual value. A rule found later that
a tool can trigger is a defect in the preview, not accepted behavior. Adding
a key to the allowlist means re-reading both functions for every place that
key is read and extending this table.

### Approval binds the values the user saw

Apply is previewed three times. The client previews and sees before and
after values. At proposal time the coordinator previews again on the GUI
thread, so an invalid patch fails at once without an approval card, and
stores that result as the confirmed set the user approves; the approval
title names the keys from it. At execution the adapter previews a third time
against the then-current config and compares every before value against the
confirmed set: a moved value is `stale_workspace`, a blocking issue is
`invalid_settings`, and neither mutates. Client-supplied values are never
trusted as before values. Where Orca normalized a value differently from the
preview, the actual value is returned and the key is listed under
`normalized`; the mutation happened, so that is a success with an honest
report.

### Registry facts worth knowing

- `ToolExecutionCoordinator::execute` dispatches on `ToolHandler` with
  explicit blocks; add a block per tool, not a generic dispatch table.
- `kInvalidatingReasons` is one global mask and includes `Settings`, so any
  pending proposal fails with `stale_revision` when the user edits a setting
  in the GUI. A per-tool mask is a later refinement if evals show friction.
- `ToolRegistry::validate_output` accepts a closed schema vocabulary: `type`,
  `properties`, `required`, `additionalProperties`, `items`, `minimum`,
  `maxItems`. Any other keyword throws; extend the validator with a test
  before using a new keyword.
- Codex CLI needs `tool_timeout_sec` raised above its 60-second default for
  approval-gated calls.

### Upstream seams the tool system owns

Two added lines in `src/CMakeLists.txt`, eight in
`src/dev-utils/platform/unix/build_linux_image.sh.in`, and one additive
`notify_project_state_changed(ProjectStateChangeReason::Settings)` call at
the end of `Plater::on_config_change`. `Plater.cpp` is the fork's busiest
file; when that function changes upstream, the natural resolution is "keep
both". No line in `Tab.cpp`, `ConfigManipulation.cpp`, or `PrintConfig.cpp`
changes; the normalizer hazards are handled by refusing the inputs in
fork-owned code.

## Proportional security growth

Keep the local baseline: automatic startup with the JusPrin Agent panel, numeric loopback binding, Origin validation, request limits, and existing mutation approval. Bearer authentication is absent: local processes with socket access can inspect exposed data and propose actions. Origin validation protects a browser boundary, not local-process identity. Do not extend this unauthenticated design to remote access.

Revisit the security design when one of these becomes true:

- the server binds beyond loopback;
- a browser or remote service must connect;
- tokens or grants must survive an application restart;
- multiple users or clients require different permissions;
- tools can read arbitrary files or sensitive account/device data;
- tools upload to a printer or begin a physical print;
- unattended or remembered approvals expand; or
- real usage makes forensic activity history a product requirement.

At that point evaluate authenticated pairing, durable credential storage, per-client grants, tool scopes, TLS/remote policy, revocation, rate controls, privacy review, and a dedicated audit log. Add them in response to the concrete exposure; do not prebuild an enterprise control plane for local v1.

Also run the shell harness with `--mcp` for direct HTTP, `--mcp-setup` for the isolated setup-command fixtures, no argument for normal shell regression, and `--stock` for stock behavior. `--manual-mcp <dedicated-temporary-directory>` provides a disposable two-plate fixture for real clients; do not use the user's normal data directory. Linux helper/launcher checks are documented in [the test README](../../tests/mcp/linux/README.md).

Executed evidence includes native read/visible approval/rejection/Undo/staleness/cancellation/shutdown checks; real Claude Code and Codex CLI reads, rejection, approval, changed-port restart and offline errors using session-only configuration; and Linux ARM64 container tests of the production helper and a compressed AppImage transport fixture. Those Linux tests are not a full GUI release image. A macOS Quit attempt during a setup fixture retained the monitor and later reaped the timed-out children; that does not prove forced OS shutdown behavior.

Still unverified: persistent one-click writes against real client installations; desktop-client read/approve/reject/restart/offline workflows (including local Cowork availability); complete Windows/Linux release packages; macOS universal signing/notarization; and remaining DPI/live-theme checks. The development macOS bundle failed strict signature verification, and the existing CI signing step is restricted to the upstream OrcaSlicer repository. Do not equate a successful local CLI test, a packaging rule, or the presence of signing identities with passing these gates.

## Definition of done

A new tool is done when:

- it fixes a named eval failure;
- its scope and authority are honest;
- the registry is the only definition source;
- the coordinator owns policy and lifecycle;
- the real operation uses Orca's current owner on the GUI thread;
- results and errors are structured and bounded;
- mutation history, approval, staleness, events, and cancellation behave as documented;
- fake, real-adapter, adapter, protocol, and shell evidence pass as applicable;
- no unrelated Orca behavior changes when the JusPrin feature is disabled; and
- the PR records any upstream seam and its rebase evidence.

Tool count is not the success metric. A compact catalog that reliably completes real printing tasks is.

# JusPrin production documentation

This directory is the canonical starting point for production work on `jusprin-newui`. It preserves the durable product and engineering decisions from `jusprin-v2-poc` without importing the POC's temporary windows, probes, static mocks, generated evidence, or environment-gated startup paths.

Read these documents in order:

1. [Product definition](product-definition.md) — the human/agent boundary, required product surfaces, workflow, and visibility rules.
2. [Production architecture](architecture.md) — the selected native/WebView architecture, ownership rules, component boundaries, and implementation sequence.
3. [Engineering and verification method](engineering-method.md) — how to assess risk and what evidence is required before calling a feature complete.
4. [OrcaSlicer integration guide](orca-integration-guide.md) — known Orca behaviors, lifecycle traps, event and history constraints, and testing lessons.
5. [Fork stewardship](fork-stewardship.md) — required before changing any OrcaSlicer-owned file: where a seam belongs, why additive beats rewritten, how to leave a conflict that resolves correctly, and what evidence a change must record.
6. [Design system](design-system.md) — brand behavior, semantic UI tokens, typography, spacing, accessibility, and asset rules.
7. [POC reference](poc-reference.md) — exact pointers to the spike-only documents, code, commits, logs, screenshots, and generated brand artifacts left on `jusprin-v2-poc`.
8. [Tool extension guide](mcp-tool-extension-guide.md) — shared Agent/MCP contracts, process-settings workflow, approval and verification requirements.

Printer UI without hardware (Bambu in-process fake; control file; isolated app): [Fake Bambu README](../../src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Testing/README.md). Print-host (Klipper/Moonraker) simulation stays on `jusprin-newui-fakeprinter`.

## Governing decisions

- JusPrin is an AI-piloted 3D-printing product built on OrcaSlicer, not a replacement slicing engine.
- OrcaSlicer's C++ model, slicing pipeline, viewport, geometry operations, project serialization, and undo stack remain authoritative.
- The production application stays native C++/wxWidgets/OpenGL. The Agent conversation uses a local React/TypeScript application inside `wxWebView`.
- JavaScript renders state and submits typed commands; it never owns editable Orca project state.
- Product policy lives in fork-owned files. OrcaSlicer-owned files receive only small, product-neutral, additive seams — every line changed there is a line this fork re-resolves at every rebase.
- The user owns physical facts, object meaning, desired outcomes, privacy and legal decisions, and authorization of consequential physical actions.
- The production branch must not import experimental POC behavior merely because it demonstrated feasibility. Use the POC as evidence and reimplement through stable production boundaries.

## Source lineage

`jusprin-newui` and `jusprin-v2-poc` share base commit `8500fcdcca` (`v2.4.2`). The POC reference is pinned to final POC commit `9bba835b92`, so future changes to branch names do not make the historical evidence ambiguous.

---

## 2.2 Physical printer setup

This surface answers: **What hardware and material will actually perform the print?**

### What should remain

- Target printer
- Nozzle diameter and nozzle type
- Build-plate type
- Loaded filament and material
- Filament color
- AMS or multi-material slot mapping
- Printer availability and current condition
- Important mismatches between configuration and observed hardware

### Why the agent cannot decide this alone

Configured state and physical state can diverge. Selecting “PLA” in software does not establish that PLA is actually loaded, dry, correctly mapped, or compatible with the installed plate and nozzle.

### What the agent should do

- Discover printers and materials automatically
- Read AMS and printer state where available
- Compare observed state with the project
- Recommend compatible profiles
- Explain mismatches
- Ask the user only about unresolved physical facts

The existing setup wizard’s enormous lists of printer and filament profiles should become hardware discovery followed by a short confirmation.

content.text:
# How the Add a Printer flow should work on the backend

Most of this flow already exists on `jusprin-newui` (commit 39c077bff8, "Add the evidence-led Add a printer flow"). It covers the text/photo box, recognition, choosing between matches, and applying the profile. My proposal keeps that design, fills the gaps against the Figma page, and adds three shared tools so the in-app chat and external AI tools (Claude Code, Codex) can add a printer too. Some of this introduces patterns the docs don't cover yet; they're listed at the end.

I read the code on `jusprin-newui` in the main checkout. This worktree is on the old v1 branch and has no `agent-docs`.

## What exists today

- **Dialog and state machine.** [PrinterSetupController.cpp](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/PrinterSetup/PrinterSetupController.cpp) is a GUI-free state machine: Initial → Recognizing → Recognized / Ambiguous / Error → Complete.
- **The LLM call.** [PrinterRecognition.cpp](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/PrinterSetup/PrinterRecognition.cpp) makes one non-streaming OpenAI Responses call with `store:false` and a strict JSON schema. It sends:
  - the user's text and optional photo;
  - a shortlist of shipped printer profiles: up to 60 text matches, or up to 400 models when there is only a photo.

  The schema limits `candidate_ids` to that shortlist, so the model can't name a printer JusPrin doesn't ship. A test version returns fixed answers with no network call.
- **Guards.** The controller throws away any ID that wasn't offered. A single match below 0.7 confidence becomes a choice the user confirms. A correction reruns recognition with "Current match / Correction" appended to the description text.
- **Apply.** `SetupCommands::install_and_select_printer` enables the vendor/model/nozzle and selects its system preset, restoring the old setup if that fails.
- **Chat agent.** The in-app chat is separate. [OpenAIResponsesAgent.cpp](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/OpenAIResponsesAgent.cpp) runs a streaming tool loop over [ToolRegistry](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ToolRegistry.hpp). Every change goes through `ToolExecutionCoordinator`, and the same registry feeds the MCP server that external AI tools connect to.

## Gaps against the Figma page

| Frame | Gap |
|---|---|
| 18a | Discovery reads `get_my_machine_list()`: printers already bound to the account or connected. A new printer on the LAN that isn't bound yet shows up only in `get_local_machinelist()`. |
| 18b | The assumed plate and material come back as free text. A correction like "it's on a smooth plate" is only reported as "Not applied". |
| 18c | Nothing reads nozzle, plate or AMS spools from the printer, and there is no access-code field. |
| 18d | The tell-them-apart hint ("the V2 has a knob") is squeezed into the `assumption` field. Adding a photo or more text isn't possible in the Ambiguous state, because `correct()` only works after a single match. |
| 18e | "Set it up myself" opens Orca's old wizard, not the model grid with nozzle chips. |
| 18f | I found no "No agent connected" state in the dialog. Without a key, recognition simply fails with "needs the OpenAI key". |
| Chat / MCP | There are no printer tools. An external AI tool can't add a printer. |

## Proposal

### 1. Keep the dialog as one structured call, not an agent turn

The dialog needs a fixed set of outcomes, bounded cost and latency, and a schema-checked answer. A chat tool loop gives none of those. So the dialog keeps its own recognition call. Changes to that call:

**Input.** Send the current match ID and the correction as their own labeled input parts, instead of pasting them into the description.

**Output schema, extended:**
```json
{
  "disposition": "recognized | ambiguous | no_match",
  "candidate_ids": ["<shortlist id>"],
  "evidence_summary": "string",
  "confidence": 0.0,
  "distinguishing_features": [{"candidate_id": "...", "feature": "knob under the screen"}],
  "stated_facts": {"nozzle_mm": "string|empty", "plate": "string|empty", "material": "string|empty"},
  "assumptions": [{"fact": "nozzle|plate|material", "value": "...", "reason": "..."}],
  "unresolved_correction": "string"
}
```

**Mapping the answer.** Deterministic C++, not the model, maps `stated_facts` onto real choices:
- a nozzle size picks a different shortlist ID;
- a plate maps through `SetupCommands::bed_types()`;
- a material maps through `compatible_filaments()`.

Anything that doesn't map shows as "Not applied". The model never names a preset, so it can't invent one.

**Refining an ambiguous result.** Add `refine(evidence)` to the controller for 18d. It reruns recognition with the extra text or photo, keeping the current candidates as the shortlist.

**Photo-only size (unverified).** A photo-only call can carry a 400-value enum. I believe OpenAI's structured outputs cap total enum size, but I haven't checked the exact limits. If evals show it's a problem, split it into two calls:
1. A small vision call extracts vendor, nameplate text and visible features.
2. That text builds the normal ≤60 text-match shortlist, and the existing recognition call runs on it.

Don't build the split before measuring.

### 2. Steps that need no LLM call at all

- **18c, network printer.** Map `printer_type` to the catalog entry. Then read the nozzle from `MachineObject::GetNozzleSystem()` and spools from `GetFilaSystem()`, and pick the nozzle variant that matches. The Figma copy "Nothing to assume" is literally true here. [PrinterSetupLauncher.cpp](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/PrinterSetup/PrinterSetupLauncher.cpp) reads the key itself: consent plus `load_provider_api_key("openai")`. I'd extract a shared client only when a second task needs one, such as spool-photo recognition.
2. **Chaining calls**, if the two-step photo path is adopted.

4. **Device data reaching AI adapters.** The guide's security section says to revisit the design when tools can read device data. That's why `printers_discover` starts in-app only and without identifiers.
5. **Product gap for users on the external-AI-tool route.** A user who connected Claude Code instead of entering an API key has no in-app model, so the dialog would show 18f even though an agent is connected. Options:
   - (a) Accept it; those users add printers by asking their tool, which uses the new MCP tools.
   - (b) Change 18f's copy for them.

Everything else extends existing seams: registry entries, a workspace command, discovery reads and controller methods.

# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## Overview

OrcaSlicer is an open-source 3D slicer application forked from Bambu Studio, built using C++ with wxWidgets for the GUI and CMake as the build system. The project uses a modular architecture with separate libraries for core slicing functionality, GUI components, and platform-specific code.

## Build Commands

### Building on Windows
```bash
# Build everything
build_release_vs2022.bat

# Build with debug symbols
build_release_vs2022.bat debug

# Build only dependencies
build_release_vs2022.bat deps

# Build only slicer (after deps are built)
build_release_vs2022.bat slicer


```

### Building on macOS
```bash
# Build everything (dependencies and slicer)
./build_release_macos.sh

# Build only dependencies
./build_release_macos.sh -d

# Build only slicer (after deps are built)
./build_release_macos.sh -s

# Use Ninja generator for faster builds
./build_release_macos.sh -x

# Build for specific architecture
./build_release_macos.sh -a arm64    # or x86_64 or universal

# Build for specific macOS version target
./build_release_macos.sh -t 11.3
```

### Building on Linux
```bash
# First time setup - install system dependencies
./build_linux.sh -u

# Build dependencies and slicer
./build_linux.sh -dsi

# Build everything (alternative)
./build_linux.sh -dsi

# Individual options:
./build_linux.sh -d    # dependencies only
./build_linux.sh -s    # slicer only  
./build_linux.sh -i    # build AppImage

# Performance and debug options:
./build_linux.sh -j N  # limit to N cores
./build_linux.sh -1    # single core build
./build_linux.sh -b    # debug build
./build_linux.sh -c    # clean build
./build_linux.sh -r    # skip RAM/disk checks
./build_linux.sh -l    # use Clang instead of GCC
```

### Build System
- Uses CMake with minimum version 3.13 (maximum 3.31.x on Windows)
- Primary build directory: `build/`
- Dependencies are built in `deps/build/`
- The build process is split into dependency building and main application building
- Windows builds use Visual Studio generators
- macOS builds use Xcode by default, Ninja with -x flag
- Linux builds use Ninja generator

### Testing
Tests are located in the `tests/` directory and use the Catch2 testing framework. Test structure:
- `tests/libslic3r/` - Core library tests (21 test files)
  - Geometry processing, algorithms, file formats (STL, 3MF, AMF)
  - Polygon operations, clipper utilities, Voronoi diagrams
- `tests/fff_print/` - Fused Filament Fabrication tests (12 test files)
  - Slicing algorithms, G-code generation, print mechanics
  - Fill patterns, extrusion, support material
- `tests/sla_print/` - Stereolithography tests (4 test files)
  - SLA-specific printing algorithms, support generation
- `tests/libnest2d/` - 2D nesting algorithm tests
- `tests/slic3rutils/` - Utility function tests
- `tests/sandboxes/` - Experimental/sandbox test code

Run all tests after building:
```bash
cd build && ctest
```

Run tests with verbose output:
```bash
cd build && ctest --output-on-failure
```

Run individual test suites:
```bash
# From build directory
./tests/libslic3r/libslic3r_tests
./tests/fff_print/fff_print_tests
./tests/sla_print/sla_print_tests
```

## Architecture

### Core Libraries
- **libslic3r/**: Core slicing engine and algorithms (platform-independent)
  - Main slicing logic, geometry processing, G-code generation
  - Key classes: Print, PrintObject, Layer, GCode, Config
  - Modular design with specialized subdirectories:
    - `GCode/` - G-code generation, cooling, pressure equalization, thumbnails
    - `Fill/` - Infill pattern implementations (gyroid, honeycomb, lightning, etc.)
    - `Support/` - Tree supports and traditional support generation
    - `Geometry/` - Advanced geometry operations, Voronoi diagrams, medial axis
    - `Format/` - File I/O for 3MF, AMF, STL, OBJ, STEP formats
    - `SLA/` - SLA-specific print processing and support generation
    - `Arachne/` - Advanced wall generation using skeletal trapezoidation

- **src/slic3r/**: Main application framework and GUI
  - GUI application built with wxWidgets
  - Integration between libslic3r core and user interface
  - Located in `src/slic3r/GUI/` (not shown in this directory but exists)

### Key Algorithmic Components
- **Arachne Wall Generation**: Variable-width perimeter generation using skeletal trapezoidation
- **Tree Supports**: Organic support generation algorithm  
- **Lightning Infill**: Sparse infill optimization for internal structures
- **Adaptive Slicing**: Variable layer height based on geometry
- **Multi-material**: Multi-extruder and soluble support processing
- **G-code Post-processing**: Cooling, fan control, pressure advance, conflict checking

### File Format Support
- **3MF/BBS_3MF**: Native format with extensions for multi-material and metadata
- **STL**: Standard tessellation language for 3D models
- **AMF**: Additive Manufacturing Format with color/material support  
- **OBJ**: Wavefront OBJ with material definitions
- **STEP**: CAD format support for precise geometry
- **G-code**: Output format with extensive post-processing capabilities

### External Dependencies
- **Clipper2**: Advanced 2D polygon clipping and offsetting
- **libigl**: Computational geometry library for mesh operations
- **TBB**: Intel Threading Building Blocks for parallelization
- **wxWidgets**: Cross-platform GUI framework
- **OpenGL**: 3D graphics rendering and visualization
- **CGAL**: Computational Geometry Algorithms Library (selective use)
- **OpenVDB**: Volumetric data structures for advanced operations
- **Eigen**: Linear algebra library for mathematical operations

## File Organization

### Resources and Configuration
- `resources/profiles/` - Printer and material profiles organized by manufacturer
- `resources/printers/` - Printer-specific configurations and G-code templates  
- `resources/images/` - UI icons, logos, calibration images
- `resources/calib/` - Calibration test patterns and data
- `resources/handy_models/` - Built-in test models (benchy, calibration cubes)

### Internationalization and Localization  
- `localization/i18n/` - Source translation files (.pot, .po)
- `resources/i18n/` - Runtime language resources
- Translation managed via `scripts/run_gettext.sh` / `scripts/run_gettext.bat`

### Platform-Specific Code
- `src/libslic3r/Platform.cpp` - Platform abstractions and utilities
- `src/libslic3r/MacUtils.mm` - macOS-specific utilities (Objective-C++)
- Windows-specific build scripts and configurations
- Linux distribution support scripts in `scripts/linux.d/`

### Build and Development Tools
- `cmake/modules/` - Custom CMake find modules and utilities
- `scripts/` - Python utilities for profile generation and validation  
- `tools/` - Windows build tools (gettext utilities)
- `deps/` - External dependency build configurations

## Development Workflow

### Code Style and Standards
- **C++17 standard** with selective C++20 features
- **Naming conventions**: PascalCase for classes, snake_case for functions/variables
- **Header guards**: Use `#pragma once` 
- **Memory management**: Prefer smart pointers, RAII patterns
- **Thread safety**: Use TBB for parallelization, be mindful of shared state

### Common Development Tasks

#### Adding New Print Settings
1. Define setting in `PrintConfig.cpp` with proper bounds and defaults
2. Add UI controls in appropriate GUI components  
3. Update serialization in config save/load
4. Add tooltips and help text for user guidance
5. Test with different printer profiles

#### Modifying Slicing Algorithms  
1. Core algorithms live in `libslic3r/` subdirectories
2. Performance-critical code should be profiled and optimized
3. Consider multi-threading implications (TBB integration)
4. Validate changes don't break existing profiles
5. Add regression tests where appropriate

#### GUI Development
1. GUI code resides in `src/slic3r/GUI/` (not visible in current tree)
2. Use existing wxWidgets patterns and custom controls
3. Support both light and dark themes
4. Consider DPI scaling on high-resolution displays
5. Maintain cross-platform compatibility

#### Adding Printer Support
1. Create JSON profile in `resources/profiles/[manufacturer].json`
2. Add printer-specific start/end G-code templates
3. Configure build volume, capabilities, and material compatibility
4. Test thoroughly with actual hardware when possible
5. Follow existing profile structure and naming conventions

### Dependencies and Build System
- **CMake-based** with separate dependency building phase
- **Dependencies** built once in `deps/build/`, then linked to main application  
- **Cross-platform** considerations important for all changes
- **Resource files** embedded at build time, platform-specific handling

### Performance Considerations
- **Slicing algorithms** are CPU-intensive, profile before optimizing
- **Memory usage** can be substantial with complex models
- **Multi-threading** extensively used via TBB
- **File I/O** optimized for large 3MF files with embedded textures
- **Real-time preview** requires efficient mesh processing

## Important Development Notes

### Codebase Navigation
- Use search tools extensively - codebase has 500k+ lines
- Key entry points: `src/OrcaSlicer.cpp` for application startup
- Core slicing: `libslic3r/Print.cpp` orchestrates the slicing pipeline
- Configuration: `PrintConfig.cpp` defines all print/printer/material settings

### Compatibility and Stability
- **Backward compatibility** maintained for project files and profiles
- **Cross-platform** support essential (Windows/macOS/Linux)  
- **File format** changes require careful version handling
- **Profile migrations** needed when settings change significantly

### Quality and Testing
- **Regression testing** important due to algorithm complexity
- **Performance benchmarks** help catch performance regressions
- **Memory leak** detection important for long-running GUI application
- **Cross-platform** testing required before releases

- [jusprin-v2-poc rebase, not merge](jusprin-v2-poc-rebase-not-merge.md) — branch forks from release/v2.4; rebase only the fork's commits (2 conflicts) instead of merging upstream in (531).
- [Verify before claiming rebase risk](fork-rebase-risk-verify-before-claiming.md) — three checks that would have caught three wrong confident claims in a fork audit.
- [Phase 1 shell wraps the intact Notebook](jusprin-shell-phase-1-design.md) — hide the tab strip, don't reparent Plater; sidebar policy seam; evidence doc location.
- [Inherited teardown crash](orca-inherited-teardown-crash.md) — exiting with volumes loaded segfaults in ~GLCanvas3D via destroyed Plater priv; predates the shell.

## Architecture

### Core Libraries
- **libslic3r/**: Core slicing engine and algorithms (platform-independent)
  - Main slicing logic, geometry processing, G-code generation
  - Key classes: Print, PrintObject, Layer, GCode, Config
  - Modular design with specialized subdirectories:
    - `GCode/` - G-code generation, cooling, pressure equalization, thumbnails
    - `Fill/` - Infill pattern implementations (gyroid, honeycomb, lightning, etc.)
    - `Support/` - Tree supports and traditional support generation
    - `Geometry/` - Advanced geometry operations, Voronoi diagrams, medial axis
    - `Format/` - File I/O for 3MF, AMF, STL, OBJ, STEP formats
    - `SLA/` - SLA-specific print processing and support generation
    - `Arachne/` - Advanced wall generation using skeletal trapezoidation

- **src/slic3r/**: Main application framework and GUI
  - GUI application built with wxWidgets
  - Integration between libslic3r core and user interface
  - Located in `src/slic3r/GUI/` (not shown in this directory but exists)

### Key Algorithmic Components
- **Arachne Wall Generation**: Variable-width perimeter generation using skeletal trapezoidation
- **Tree Supports**: Organic support generation algorithm  
- **Lightning Infill**: Sparse infill optimization for internal structures
- **Adaptive Slicing**: Variable layer height based on geometry
- **Multi-material**: Multi-extruder and soluble support processing
- **G-code Post-processing**: Cooling, fan control, pressure advance, conflict checking

### File Format Support
- **3MF/BBS_3MF**: Native format with extensions for multi-material and metadata
- **STL**: Standard tessellation language for 3D models
- **AMF**: Additive Manufacturing Format with color/material support  
- **OBJ**: Wavefront OBJ with material definitions
- **STEP**: CAD format support for precise geometry
- **G-code**: Output format with extensive post-processing capabilities

### External Dependencies
- **Clipper2**: Advanced 2D polygon clipping and offsetting
- **libigl**: Computational geometry library for mesh operations
- **TBB**: Intel Threading Building Blocks for parallelization
- **wxWidgets**: Cross-platform GUI framework
- **OpenGL**: 3D graphics rendering and visualization
- **CGAL**: Computational Geometry Algorithms Library (selective use)
- **OpenVDB**: Volumetric data structures for advanced operations
- **Eigen**: Linear algebra library for mathematical operations

## File Organization

### Resources and Configuration
- `resources/profiles/` - Printer and material profiles organized by manufacturer
- `resources/printers/` - Printer-specific configurations and G-code templates  
- `resources/images/` - UI icons, logos, calibration images
- `resources/calib/` - Calibration test patterns and data
- `resources/handy_models/` - Built-in test models (benchy, calibration cubes)

### Internationalization and Localization  
- `localization/i18n/` - Source translation files (.pot, .po)
- `resources/i18n/` - Runtime language resources
- Translation managed via `scripts/run_gettext.sh` / `scripts/run_gettext.bat`

### Platform-Specific Code
- `src/libslic3r/Platform.cpp` - Platform abstractions and utilities
- `src/libslic3r/MacUtils.mm` - macOS-specific utilities (Objective-C++)
- Windows-specific build scripts and configurations
- Linux distribution support scripts in `scripts/linux.d/`

### Build and Development Tools
- `cmake/modules/` - Custom CMake find modules and utilities
- `scripts/` - Python utilities for profile generation and validation  
- `tools/` - Windows build tools (gettext utilities)
- `deps/` - External dependency build configurations

## Development Workflow

### Code Style and Standards
- **C++17 standard** with selective C++20 features
- **Naming conventions**: PascalCase for classes, snake_case for functions/variables
- **Header guards**: Use `#pragma once` 
- **Memory management**: Prefer smart pointers, RAII patterns
- **Thread safety**: Use TBB for parallelization, be mindful of shared state

### Common Development Tasks

#### Adding New Print Settings
1. Define setting in `PrintConfig.cpp` with proper bounds and defaults
2. Add UI controls in appropriate GUI components  
3. Update serialization in config save/load
4. Add tooltips and help text for user guidance
5. Test with different printer profiles

#### Modifying Slicing Algorithms  
1. Core algorithms live in `libslic3r/` subdirectories
2. Performance-critical code should be profiled and optimized
3. Consider multi-threading implications (TBB integration)
4. Validate changes don't break existing profiles
5. Add regression tests where appropriate

#### GUI Development
1. GUI code resides in `src/slic3r/GUI/` (not visible in current tree)
2. Use existing wxWidgets patterns and custom controls
3. Support both light and dark themes
4. Consider DPI scaling on high-resolution displays
5. Maintain cross-platform compatibility

#### Adding Printer Support
1. Create JSON profile in `resources/profiles/[manufacturer].json`
2. Add printer-specific start/end G-code templates
3. Configure build volume, capabilities, and material compatibility
4. Test thoroughly with actual hardware when possible
5. Follow existing profile structure and naming conventions

### Dependencies and Build System
- **CMake-based** with separate dependency building phase
- **Dependencies** built once in `deps/build/`, then linked to main application  
- **Cross-platform** considerations important for all changes
- **Resource files** embedded at build time, platform-specific handling

### Performance Considerations
- **Slicing algorithms** are CPU-intensive, profile before optimizing
- **Memory usage** can be substantial with complex models
- **Multi-threading** extensively used via TBB
- **File I/O** optimized for large 3MF files with embedded textures
- **Real-time preview** requires efficient mesh processing

## Important Development Notes

### Codebase Navigation
- Use search tools extensively - codebase has 500k+ lines
- Key entry points: `src/OrcaSlicer.cpp` for application startup
- Core slicing: `libslic3r/Print.cpp` orchestrates the slicing pipeline
- Configuration: `PrintConfig.cpp` defines all print/printer/material settings

### Compatibility and Stability
- **Backward compatibility** maintained for project files and profiles
- **Cross-platform** support essential (Windows/macOS/Linux)  
- **File format** changes require careful version handling
- **Profile migrations** needed when settings change significantly

### Quality and Testing
- **Regression testing** important due to algorithm complexity
- **Performance benchmarks** help catch performance regressions
- **Memory leak** detection important for long-running GUI application
- **Cross-platform** testing required before releases

content.text:
Yes, both device lists are upstream OrcaSlicer, and yes, you have the direction right: a tool is code the model calls, and a tool never calls a model. The "fuzzy" part of a search belongs to the model, which turns "the small bambu one" into a concrete query. The tool itself only needs forgiving string matching, and Orca already has a matcher for that. Below, screen by screen: which steps need a model, whether that model call is doable, and which existing function supplies each piece of data.

## Your two questions

**Upstream or not.** `get_my_machine_list()` and `get_local_machinelist()` are both in OrcaSlicer v2.4.2, the commit the fork started from (8500fcdcca). No fork commit has touched `DevManager.h/.cpp` since. The fork's `PrinterDiscovery.cpp` is a 28-line wrapper around `get_my_machine_list()`.

**Fuzzy search and tools.** There are two call directions, and each screen uses one:
- **The dialog calls the model.** The app sends the user's words or photo plus the printer list, and gets back a structured answer. This is what `OpenAIPrinterRecognition` already does. It is not a tool.
- **The model calls the app.** In the chat pane, or in Claude Code or Codex over MCP, the model decides to call `printers_search("Bambu Lab A1 mini")`. The tool is plain C++ string matching. The model handles vagueness by rewriting the query and calling again.

For the string matching, Orca ships `fts::fuzzy_match` ([fts_fuzzy_match.h](src/slic3r/GUI/fts_fuzzy_match.h)), which its settings search in `Search.cpp` already uses. The tool can reuse it without changes.

The dialog may not need a search step at all. The shipped catalog is only 326 printer models from 56 vendors, 785 counting nozzle sizes. At model level, without nozzle sizes, my rough estimate is 5–7k tokens: small enough to send the whole list on every call. The current code instead picks a shortlist by matching words and lists the IDs in the schema, allowing up to 400. Sending everything and checking the returned ID in C++ is simpler, and the controller already does that check.

## Which screens need a model

| Screen | User input | Needs a model? | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| 18a Initial | free text, or a photo | **yes** | natural-language or image identification |
| 18a "Use this" on a network printer | a click | no | the printer reports its own model ID |
| 18b Recognized, correction box | "I put a 0.6 nozzle on it" | **yes** | natural language into structured facts |
| 18c Network Selected | access code | no | device data plus Orca's connect path |
| 18d Ambiguous, "say more / add a photo" | text or photo | **yes** | same call as 18a, with the candidates narrowed |
| 18d "This one" / "Neither" | a click | no | |
| 18e Set it up myself | vendor dropdown, grid, nozzle chips | no | catalog listing |
| 18f No agent | clicks only | no | network list plus manual setup |

## The model calls, and whether each is doable

These are my assessments, not measurements. Each needs an eval set of real descriptions and photos before anyone relies on it.

1. **Text → printer model (18a, 18d).** Doable. Named models ("A1 mini", "X1C") should be reliable. Vague descriptions ("the small bambu one") should come back ambiguous, which is the designed outcome, not a failure. The model must never pick the nozzle size; C++ picks the model's default or a size the user stated.
2. **Photo → printer model (18a, 18d).** Partly doable.
   - A nameplate or a box photo is mostly text reading, so I expect it to work well.
   - A photo of the printer should work for distinctive shapes, like an enclosed P1S versus an open A1.
   - Near-identical siblings, like the Ender-3 V2 versus the V2 Neo, are uncertain.

   A photo can't show nozzle size. Photos are the least certain call and need the eval most.
3. **Correction → structured facts (18b).** Doable. The model extracts `{nozzle_mm, plate, material, accessories}`, and C++ maps each onto a real choice or reports "Not applied".
4. **"How to tell them apart" hint (18d, "the V2 has a knob").** Doable to generate, but risky. The shipped profiles contain nothing about how printers look, so the model writes this from its own knowledge and may invent a difference. Options:
   - label the hint as a suggestion;
   - drop it and ask for a photo of the front instead.

   This is a product call.

## What the app provides, and what already exists

"Upstream" means OrcaSlicer code the fork hasn't changed.

| Info or action | Screens | Existing function | Source | Wrapper needed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Printer catalog: vendor, model, device model ID, nozzle sizes, default materials, unsupported bed types | 18a, 18b, 18d, 18e, tools | `VendorProfile::PrinterModel`, loaded by `PresetBundle::load_vendor_configs_from_json` (and by ConfigWizard's `BundleMap::load`) | upstream | Thin. The fork's `PrinterCatalog.cpp` (228 lines) currently re-parses the same profile JSON itself. Build volume is not on `PrinterModel`, so it still has to be read from the machine preset. I haven't checked whether `BundleMap` is reachable from outside ConfigWizard. |
| Cover image | 18b, 18c, 18e | `<vendor>/<model>_cover.png` in the profiles folder | upstream resource | none |
| Forgiving name match for a search tool | chat/MCP tool | `fts::fuzzy_match` | upstream | thin loop over the catalog |
| Printers bound to the account or connected | 18a, 18f | `DeviceManager::get_my_machine_list()` | upstream | already wrapped (`PrinterDiscovery`) |
| New LAN printers, not yet bound | 18a, 18f | `DeviceManager::get_local_machinelist()`, filled by Orca's own network discovery in `GUI_App` | upstream | same wrapper, one more loop |
| Connected device → installed preset (model plus nozzle) | 18c | `get_printer_preset(const MachineObject*)`, public in `Plater.hpp`, used by Orca's "Sync printer information" | upstream | none. It only searches **installed** system presets, so a brand-new printer must be installed first. |
| Device nozzle diameter | 18c | `GetNozzleSystem()->GetNozzles()[i].m_diameter` (zero until the printer reports it) | upstream | thin read |
| AMS spools: type, color, preset ID, loaded | 18c | `GetFilaSystem()` trays: `m_fila_type`, `color`, `setting_id`, `is_exists` | upstream | thin read, display only |
| Apply AMS spools to the project | after 18c | `Sidebar::sync_ams_list` | upstream | **not directly reusable**: it opens warning dialogs, so it can't run silently from a tool |
| Build plate from the printer | 18c | none found; `DevBed.h` has no plate type | — | The Figma copy ("Textured PEI" read from the printer) isn't backed by data. The plate would come from the profile's default bed type, so the copy should say it's assumed. |
| Access code / LAN connect | 18c | `MachineObject::set_user_access_code` (what `ConnectPrinterDialog` calls); `InputIpAddressDialog` for manual IP | upstream | thin, or open Orca's dialog |
| Install and select a printer | 18b, 18c, 18e | `PresetBundle::apply_vendor_config` → `find_system_preset_by_model_and_variant` → `Tab::select_preset` | upstream | already wrapped with rollback (`SetupCommands::install_and_select_printer`) |
| Bed type choices and selection | 18b correction | `Sidebar::set_bed_type_accord_combox` | upstream | already wrapped (`bed_types`, `select_bed_type`) |
| Compatible filaments and selection | 18b correction | Orca's `is_compatible` flag and preset-switch sequence | upstream | already wrapped (`compatible_filaments`, `select_filament_preset`) |
| Manual setup | 18e | `ConfigWizard` (what "Set it up myself" opens today) | upstream | none if the old wizard stays. The Figma grid would be catalog plus install, both already listed. |
| Model API call and key | 18a, 18b, 18d | `IAgentHttpTransport`, `load_provider_api_key` | fork | exists |

## What this means for testing

- **Everything except the three model calls already exists in upstream Orca.** Most is wrapped by the fork already; the new work is thin reads of nozzle, spool and local-printer data.
- **The two new maintenance costs** are `PrinterCatalog` duplicating Orca's profile loader, and the plate data 18c promises but the printer doesn't send.
- **Device lists without hardware.** The fork's in-process fake Bambu agent (`Testing/FakeBambuAgent`) already overrides `start_discovery` and sets an access code. It may be able to fill the local printer list without a real printer, but I haven't checked what it actually sends.

content.text:
Not quite. Nothing in Orca does the searching. JusPrin narrows the printer list with its own simple word matching, then makes **one** OpenAI call that picks from that list. Orca's existing functions only come in at the very end, to install and select the chosen printer. There is no tool loop: the app calls the model once and reads back a structured answer.

## Step by step

**1. When the dialog opens**
- JusPrin reads the printer profile files that ship with the app (`resources/profiles/*.json`). It builds a flat list of every printer model and nozzle size: 785 entries such as "Bambu Lab A1 mini, 0.4 mm". Each entry gets a throwaway ID like `printer-12` that only lasts while the dialog is open.
- It asks Orca's device manager (`get_my_machine_list`) for printers that are online, and shows them under "Found on your network".

**2. If the user clicks "Use this" on a network printer**
- No model call. The printer reports its model code, JusPrin finds the catalog entry with the same code, and jumps straight to the confirmation screen.

**3. If the user types a description and/or drops a photo, then clicks Next**

*a. Build a shortlist.* JusPrin scores every catalog entry against the typed words:
- +3 for each shared word of 4 or more letters, +1 for shorter shared words;
- +20 if the full model name appears in the text.

If anything scores above zero, the top 60 become the shortlist, nozzle variants included. If nothing matches, which covers a photo alone or vague text like "the small one", the shortlist is instead one entry per model, up to 400.

*b. Check that the model can be used.* The user must have allowed cloud access and saved an OpenAI key in the Agent panel. If not, the dialog shows an error saying recognition needs the key, and the network list and manual setup still work.

*c. Make one OpenAI request.* It uses the Responses API, not streaming, with the model the Agent panel is set to (default `gpt-5.4-mini`). The request contains:
- instructions: identify the printer only from the user's evidence; return one printer only when the model is clearly identified; return two or three when it isn't; a photo doesn't prove nozzle size, so use the standard nozzle unless the user names one; never return an ID outside the list;
- the user's text plus the shortlist as JSON (ID, vendor, model, nozzle size, build volume, and whether it's the standard nozzle);
- the photo, if any, embedded as base64 image data;
- a strict answer format: a verdict (`recognized`, `ambiguous` or `no_match`), up to 3 IDs that must come from the shortlist, a one-line summary of the evidence, the assumption made (for example "assuming 0.4 mm nozzle"), a confidence from 0 to 1, and any part of a correction that couldn't be applied.

The request runs on a background thread, and a timer in the dialog checks for the answer. If the user starts over or retries meanwhile, any late answer to the old request is ignored.

**4. When the answer comes back**
- IDs that weren't on the shortlist, and duplicates, are thrown away.
- **One printer, verdict "recognized", confidence at least 0.7:** the "Recognized" screen (18b) shows the printer and the model's assumption text.
- **Two or more printers, or a single printer with low confidence:** the "Ambiguous" screen (18d) shows cards, and the user picks one. The app never assumes in this case.
- **Nothing usable:** an error saying the evidence didn't match a supported profile, with a pointer to manual setup.
- **HTTP errors:** a bad key is reported as not retryable; rate limits, server errors and network failures offer Retry, which repeats only the step that failed.

**5. If the user types a correction on the Recognized screen ("I put a 0.6 nozzle on it")**
- The whole request from step 3 runs again. The original text gets two added lines, "Current match: Bambu Lab A1 mini 0.4 mm nozzle" and "Correction: I put a 0.6 nozzle on it", and any photo is kept.
- If the correction can be expressed as a different catalog entry, like another nozzle size, the model returns that entry.
- Anything that can't be expressed that way, like a plate, material or accessory, comes back in the "couldn't apply" field and is shown as "Not applied".

**6. When the user clicks "Add this printer"**

`SetupCommands::install_and_select_printer` calls existing Orca functions:
1. It enables that model and nozzle size, plus its default filament, in the app config (`apply_vendor_config`).
2. It finds the matching system preset (`find_system_preset_by_model_and_variant`) and selects it in the printer settings tab.
3. It tells Orca the configuration changed.

If any step fails, it restores the previous config and the previous printer selection.

- **Tests and design previews** swap the OpenAI call for a fake recognizer (`DeterministicPrinterRecognition`, turned on with `JUSPRIN_PRINTER_RECOGNITION_MOCK`). It uses the same word matching and has canned answers for the Figma scenarios.
- **Text plus a photo:** the shortlist is built from the text only, so a misleading word can push the right printer off the list before the model sees the photo.
- **The "no agent connected" screen (18f)** isn't built; a missing key just shows the error from step 3b. "Set it up myself" opens Orca's old setup wizard, not the Figma model grid.

content.text:
Starting from scratch, I'd still use one structured model call per user action, not an agent that loops over tools. But I'd change what goes into the call and what comes out:
- **In:** the whole catalog, the printers found on the network, and the conversation so far, instead of a word-matched shortlist and pasted-together text.
- **Out:** every physical fact labeled with where it came from, not just printer IDs and a free-text assumption.

The app still does everything the model shouldn't: finding devices, checking IDs against the real catalog, choosing defaults, and installing.

None of this is measured yet. It's my design judgment about what current models are good and bad at, and it needs an eval before anyone relies on it.

## What current models change about the design

- **The catalog fits in one request.** 326 models is roughly 5–7k tokens. Pre-filtering only adds a way to lose the right answer, as when a vague phrase or a photo can't match words. Because the catalog is the same on every call, it can sit at the start of the prompt, where the provider's prompt caching makes it cheap and fast to resend.
- **Models are better at printer names than word matching is.** They know "X1C" means X1 Carbon, that "Ender 3 V2 Neo" is its own model, and that a "Combo" is a printer bundled with an AMS. So the model should choose from the real list directly.
- **Reading text in photos works well; telling look-alikes apart by shape doesn't.** Nameplates, box labels, the printer's screen and stickers are strong evidence. Telling near-identical models apart by appearance is where a model will sound sure and be wrong.
- **A model's own confidence number is not reliable.** A better signal is whether the answer quotes evidence ("the user wrote A1 mini", "the nameplate reads P1S") or was only inferred.
- **Tool loops cost time and predictability.** They pay off when the data is large, changes during the task, or is expensive to fetch. Here all the data is small and known before the call, so give it to the model up front.

## The design

**1. Collect free, reliable evidence first.** Run network discovery before the user types anything. A printer on the network reports its model, nozzle and loaded spools, which beats any guess. If exactly one new printer is found, suggest it immediately.

**2. Treat the dialog as a short conversation with one model.** Every user action is a new turn: the first description, an added photo, a correction, "neither of these", an answer to a question. Every request includes:
- a fixed prefix: instructions, then the full catalog with each model's stable ID, name, nozzle sizes and supported plates;
- the printers currently found on the network, with the data they report;
- all earlier turns, and the model's own earlier answers.

A correction is then just the next message, not text appended to the original description.

**3. The model returns the whole current state each turn,** and the app draws the screen from it:

```json
{
  "status": "identified | choose | need_more | not_in_catalog",
  "candidates": [{"model_id": "BBL/Bambu Lab A1 mini", "evidence": "user wrote 'A1 mini'",
                  "evidence_kind": "stated | read_in_photo | appearance | network_device"}],
  "question": "Is there a knob under the screen?",
  "facts": [{"fact": "nozzle_mm", "value": "0.6", "source": "stated"},
            {"fact": "accessory", "value": "AMS lite", "source": "stated"}],
  "outside_catalog": {"name": "Sovol SV08", "note": "not in the shipped profiles"}
}
```

The rules this encodes:
- **Every fact names its source.** The app only treats a fact as confirmed when it was stated, read in a photo, or reported by the device. Anything else is shown as an assumption, which matches the product rule that the user owns physical facts.
- **When unsure, ask the one question that separates the candidates, or ask for a specific photo** ("the front", "the label on the back"). Don't state how the models differ as fact; a wrong question costs one reply, while a made-up difference misleads.
- **If the printer isn't in the catalog, say what it probably is** and send the user to manual setup. Today that case is a dead end.
- **If the description matches a printer on the network,** return that device, so nozzle and spools come from the printer instead of guesses.

**4. The app checks and fills in, without the model.**
- Throw away any model ID that isn't in the catalog.
- Pick the nozzle size: stated or reported by the device, else the model's standard one.
- Map plate and material facts onto that model's actual options. Anything that doesn't map is shown as "Not applied".

The screen type comes from the answer's structure, not a confidence number. The user always clicks "Add this printer" at the end, so the model's answer can never install anything by itself.

**5. Install through the normal preset path.** Unchanged.

## Where tools belong

Tools belong in the chat pane and in external AI clients over MCP. There the model is already holding a conversation, so letting it call tools is natural. Those tools would be:
- `printers_catalog`: the catalog, optionally filtered by vendor. It's small enough that no fuzzy search is needed.
- `printers_on_network`
- `printer_add`: requires approval

Both entry points share the catalog, discovery and install code; only the direction of the calls differs.

## Compared with today's implementation

| Today | From scratch |
|---|---|
| Word-matched shortlist of 60 or 400 entries | Full catalog, cached at the start of the prompt |
| IDs for each model-and-nozzle pair, reset each time the dialog opens | Stable model IDs; the app picks the nozzle |
| Network printers kept separate from recognition | Network printers included as evidence |
| Correction pasted into the description text | Conversation turns |
| Plate and material corrections always "Not applied" | Mapped onto the chosen model's real options |
| Ambiguous screen decided by a confidence of 0.7 | Decided by the kind of evidence; the model asks a question |
| Model writes the differences as fact | Model asks a question or requests a specific photo |
| No-match is a dead end | Names the likely printer and offers manual setup |

## What has to be proven before building it

An eval set covering:
- typed names, vague descriptions, nameplate photos, box photos, front photos of look-alikes;
- corrections;
- printers that aren't in the catalog.

Measure four things:
1. how often the right printer is picked on the first answer;
2. how often the app **should** have asked but didn't (the dangerous failure);
3. how many turns it takes to finish;
4. latency and cost with the catalog cached.

The main open risk is photo-only identification of look-alike models. If the eval shows it's unreliable, the design still holds: such cases just end up asking a question or requesting a label photo more often.

content.text:
The current implementation is simpler. My proposal does more: it adds three screen states (ask a question, not in the catalog, printer found on the network), labels every fact with its source, and applies plate and material corrections. Each of those is new code, and the model makes more of the decisions, so more behavior has to be tested.

Some parts of the proposal, though, would make today's code **smaller** without adding any feature. Those are worth doing on their own.

## Changes that remove code

| Change | What goes away |
|---|---|
| Send the whole catalog instead of a shortlist | The word-scoring shortlist in `PrinterCatalog::recognition_choices` (~30 lines), the 60/400 split, and the bug where text pushes the right printer off the list before the model sees the photo. The strict answer format would also stop listing every allowed ID; the controller already rejects unknown IDs. |
| Stop using the confidence number to choose a screen | One branch and the 0.7 constant in `PrinterSetupController`. The user confirms before anything is installed, so the number never protected against a wrong install. |
| One catalog entry per model; C++ picks the nozzle | The prompt's nozzle rules and the per-entry "standard nozzle" flag. This moves a little logic into C++, since "I put a 0.6 nozzle on it" must map to a nozzle size, so it's closer to neutral than a pure win. |

## Changes that add code

| Change | What it adds | In the Figma design? |
|---|---|---|
| Facts labeled with their source; plate and material corrections applied | Mapping to each model's plate and filament options, plus showing them on screen | Partly: 18b shows assumptions and a correction box, but not how corrections apply |
| Network printers included in the model's evidence | Logic to merge device data with the model's answer | No |
| The model asks a question or requests a photo | A new screen state | No; 18d shows the model's description of the differences |
| "Probably X, not in the catalog" | A new screen state | No |
| Conversation turns instead of pasted text | Stored history resent on every request. About the same size as today's approach, but less fragile: the test recognizer currently has to parse the pasted "Current match:" marker. | — |

## Recommendation

Keep the current structure and make the three code-removing changes. Add the others only when an eval shows a real failure, for example users correcting the plate often, or look-alike printers getting identified wrongly. Three of the additions aren't in the Figma design at all, so building them now would mean building features nobody has asked for yet.

---
name: jusprin-worktree-build
description: How to configure a JusPrin worktree build reusing existing deps; BUILD_TESTS=ON needed for tests
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
  originSessionId: 01c34c35-1546-40fb-a600-c49b2e1ffa06
  modified: 2026-09-02T19:01:12.232Z
---

A JusPrin git worktree builds against the already-built deps by configuring:

```
cmake -B build/arm64 -G "Ninja Multi-Config" -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DCMAKE_OSX_ARCHITECTURES=arm64 -DCMAKE_OSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET=15.0 \
  -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/deps/build/arm64/OrcaSlicer_dep/usr/local;/Users/kenneth/Projects/OrcaSlicer/deps/build/arm64/OrcaSlicer_dep/usr/local" \
  -DSLIC3R_GUI=ON -DSLIC3R_STATIC=ON -DSLIC3R_PCH=ON -DBUILD_TESTS=ON
```

`BUILD_TESTS=ON` is required or the tests/ tree (workspace, shell targets) is
not generated. Build with `cmake --build build/arm64 --config RelWithDebInfo
--target <targets>`. wxWidgets 3.3 sources for API verification live under
/Users/kenneth/Projects/OrcaSlicer/deps/build/arm64/dep_wxWidgets-prefix/.

CWD TRAP (cost real time once): the harness resets the Bash cwd to the main
repo /Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin between turns, so a *relative*
`cmake --build build/arm64` silently builds the MAIN repo's build dir, not the
worktree's — the worktree binary then runs stale code and a re-fix looks like it
"didn't take". Always pass the worktree build dir as an ABSOLUTE path to
`cmake --build /…/.claude/worktrees/<wt>/build/arm64 …`, and run test binaries by
absolute path. Also: `cmake --build --target <one_exe>` may relink against a
stale lib without recompiling a changed .cpp in that lib — build the app target
(e.g. OrcaSlicer) too so the lib recompiles; verify with
`grep -c '<file>.cpp.o' build.log`. Editing tools (Edit/Write) use absolute
paths so source edits land correctly regardless of cwd.

description: "RelWithDebInfo liblibslic3r_gui.a crossed Apple ar's 4 GiB archive limit on jusprin-newui (2026-09-13); CMAKE_AR override is ignored; manual llvm-ar relink recipe and its cd trap"

On 2026-09-13, at jusprin-newui 770bd2b0a2 (after "Add the evidence-led Add a
printer flow"), a worktree RelWithDebInfo build failed archiving
`src/slic3r/RelWithDebInfo/liblibslic3r_gui.a`:
`Assertion failed: (memberOffset < 0xFFFFFFFF) ... ArchiveWriter.cpp` then
`fatal error in .../ranlib`. The archive llvm-ar produced was 4,309,350,176
bytes; the main checkout's copy built minutes earlier was 4,143,827,796 and
still fit. Objects are big because the root CMakeLists.txt (lines ~544-548)
rewrites RelWithDebInfo -O2 to -O0 on purpose. Disk space was not the cause.

**Why:** the failed build left the OLD harness binary in place, and the harness
runs afterwards "passed" against stale code (a new `--printer-setup` flag
silently ran the default mode: same 285 check count). Gate runs on build
success and compare binary mtime.

**How to apply:**
- `-DCMAKE_AR=/opt/homebrew/opt/llvm/bin/llvm-ar` on an existing build dir does
  nothing: `CMakeFiles/<ver>/CMakeCXXCompiler.cmake` sets CMAKE_AR as a normal
  variable that shadows the cache.
- Working relink: `ninja -f build-RelWithDebInfo.ninja -t commands <target>`,
  drop compile lines, swap ar/ranlib for llvm-ar/llvm-ranlib on the gui archive
  line only, then run EACH line in its own `(cd build/arm64 && eval "$line")`.
  One `sh` script fails with bogus "no such file" errors because the
  encoding-check line does `cd src/slic3r` and it leaks; `sh -e` also does not
  stop inside `&&` chains. Apple's linker accepted the >4 GiB llvm-ar archive.
- A lasting fix (llvm-ar in the toolchain, thin archives, or less debug info)
  is Kenneth's call; the main checkout will hit this on its next growth.
